title: Backpressure and flow control
subtitle: When the consumer is slower than the producer, you must buffer, drop or slow the sender. Learn to slow the sender, so your queues stay small.

c.v: On 25 March 2026, voice and video on Discord were badly degraded from 12:13 to 15:30 PDT. Most users could not start or join calls. They saw "Awaiting Endpoint".
It began with a routine config change. Kubernetes stopped pods before their sessions could hand off cleanly. About 17% of sessions across Discord stopped without warning.
Those users all tried to reconnect. Discord has a start-session
when we have a flood of requests". But that limit had not been re-tuned after a recent migration. Too many session starts got through, and gateway nodes in one zone began to run out of memory.
The voice service had a second problem. Its Elixir processes read one message at a time from a mailbox, "a queue of incoming messages".

Each new outbound connection went through a single supervisor process. To start a process, that supervisor scanned its mailbox for one message. With about 100,000 messages waiting, each start took about 1 ms longer.

So the longer the queue got, the slower it drained. In total, the mailboxes on 15 voice syncers grew to nearly 1 million messages and kept rising. The connection that sends health reports to etcd also went through those supervisors. After the 60-second
Early restarts helped only briefly, because the queues filled again. Recovery came after the team set lower spawn limits and doubled the instances.
does it. Sometimes the producer is faster for a while. What then?
You have three choices, and only three:
Store the extra work and do it later.
Throw some work away, on purpose.
Make the sender wait until the consumer is ready.
. The slow part pushes back on the fast part. A buffer only buys time. If the producer stays faster on average, the buffer fills, and then you are back to choosing between dropping and slowing.
is choice 2: drop work early and cheaply. Backpressure is choice 3. You often need both. You can slow your own services, but you cannot slow a user who is tapping a button.
A queue does not add capacity. It only moves the wait. Give every queue a limit, and decide what happens when it is full: the sender waits, or the sender gets an error.
Many queues have no limit by default. In Python,
, and that means "the queue size is infinite".
The Java docs say what this means. An unbounded queue smooths out short bursts. But it allows "unbounded work queue growth" when tasks keep arriving faster than they finish.
lesson showed, a long queue also means a long wait for every item in it.

Node.js measured the cost. It compressed a file of about 9 GB with streams, once with backpressure and once without. With backpressure, the process used about 87.81 MB of memory. Without it, about 1.52 GB.
has a fixed size. Java's docs say it "helps prevent resource exhaustion".
The hard part is the next question: what happens when it is full?
When a bounded queue is full, the producer either waits or gets an error. Pick one on purpose.
Here is both, in a small sketch:

blocks.v:
import asyncio

queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)  # at most 100 jobs wait (Python 3.10+)

async def producer(jobs):
    for job in jobs:
        await queue.put(job)  # waits while the queue is full

async def worker():
    while True:
        job = await queue.get()
        try:
            await handle(job)
        finally:
            queue.task_done()

def enqueue_from_request(job):  # a handler that must not wait
    try:
        queue.put_nowait(job)
        return 202
    except asyncio.QueueFull:
        return 503  # caller should back off and retry later

Pull and credits instead of push
In a push system, the sender decides the rate. Kafka's docs say a push consumer "tends to be overwhelmed" when it is slower than the producer.
So Kafka consumers pull. A slow consumer "simply falls behind and catches up when it can".

How backpressure travels, and where it stops
Backpressure works best when it travels back, hop by hop, to whoever started the work. Step through it. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
The chain is only as good as its weakest link. Three things break it:
The signal stops there. That part just grows. In Discord's outage, the mailboxes kept growing until the team lowered rate limits upstream.
An async boundary that answers early.
"202 Accepted" ends the caller's wait before the work is done. From then on, only the queue's limit protects you. Reactive Streams exists to carry the signal across exactly these boundaries.
A call nobody waits for can never slow anybody down.

q.v: A service creates its worker pool with Java's Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8). Jobs arrive faster than 8 threads can finish them, for an hour. What happens?

options.v: New jobs are rejected with RejectedExecutionException once all 8 threads are busy.
The pool starts more threads to keep up.
New jobs wait in a queue with no size limit, which keeps growing and uses more and more memory.

why.v: newFixedThreadPool uses a shared unbounded queue. A running pool rejects jobs only when both its threads and its queue have finite limits and are full.

q.v: In Reactive Streams, a subscriber has called request(10) and has received 10 items. What may the publisher do next?

options.v: Send more items, as long as it sends them slowly.
Wait. It may not send more items until the subscriber requests more.
Drop the subscription, because the demand is used up.

why.v: The total number of items sent must never be more than the total requested. Demand is a credit, and the subscriber gives more credit with another request(n).

q.v: An API puts each request on a queue and returns 202 Accepted at once. A worker reads the queue. The worker slows down. Which statement is true?

options.v: The client slows down too, because backpressure always travels back to the caller.
The client does not slow down. The queue absorbs the difference, so you must give it a limit and decide what happens when it is full.
The worker's TCP window will make the client wait.

why.v: The 202 ends the client's wait before the work is done. That async boundary stops backpressure. Only a limit on the queue, with a wait or a reject, brings it back.

q.v: Your request handler must not wait. Which asyncio call fits a bounded queue there?

options.v: await queue.put(job), and let it wait for a free slot.
queue.put_nowait(job), and turn QueueFull into 503 with Retry-After.
asyncio.Queue() with the default maxsize, so it never fills.

why.v: put_nowait raises QueueFull at once when the queue is at maxsize. The default maxsize of 0 means the queue has no limit.
